screens.title: Upgradable Smart Contracts and Proxies
screens.subtitle: How to evolve logic while preserving on-chain state and address

narration.text: Blockchains make deployed smart contracts immutable. That immutability is valuable for trust, but it becomes a problem when a bug or new requirement appears. In this lesson you'll learn why upgradability is a practical pattern, without pretending the contract itself can be changed. The key idea is to separate state from logic: a proxy holds storage at a fixed address and delegates execution to an implementation contract that can be swapped. This maintains the same user-facing address and preserves balances, ownership, and other stored data. We will study two common proxy patterns — the Transparent Proxy and UUPS — and see how OpenZeppelin's Upgrades plugin for Hardhat simplifies deployment and safety checks. You will also learn the storage-compatibility rules you must follow and the trade-offs in centralization, complexity, and attack surface. Concrete examples will include deployment and upgrade scripts, a V1 to V2 walkthrough, and common mistakes to avoid. By the end, you'll understand when upgradability is appropriate, how delegatecall works in practice, and how to use the OpenZeppelin tooling to manage upgrades responsibly. Consider how your project's trust model would change if the owner can upgrade the logic; that trade-off frames every technical decision we cover.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Keep storage stable at a proxy address and swap logic by changing the implementation target. This preserves state and makes upgrades possible while respecting blockchain immutability.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Upgradable Smart Contracts
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Upgradable Smart Contracts and Proxies

Learn how to evolve contract logic without losing on-chain state. We'll map the proxy architecture, explain delegatecall, compare proxy patterns, and run deploy and upgrade scripts with OpenZeppelin tooling.

In this lesson
Why upgradability matters, proxy vs implementation separation, and safety rules.
Coming up
Transparent and UUPS patterns, deployment, upgrade flow.
Hands-on
Deploy BoxV1 and upgrade to BoxV2 using OpenZeppelin Upgrades.
Proxy Architecture Overview
State held at fixed address • Logic swapped via implementation pointer
Proxy
Holds storage and a pointer to implementation. Receives user calls and uses delegatecall to run logic.
Implementation
Deployable logic contracts. New versions can be swapped in without moving storage.
Quick flow
  1. Deploy proxy at a fixed address and initial implementation.
  2. Proxy delegates calls with delegatecall, keeping storage in proxy.
  3. When ready, deploy new implementation and update proxy pointer.
Key Takeaway

Upgrades preserve address and state by swapping implementation logic while proxy storage remains unchanged.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will gain four practical competencies. First, you will understand immutability: why deployed contracts cannot be rewritten and what that means for long-lived applications. Knowing this helps you reason about risk when design choices require flexibility. Second, you will be able to explain proxy-based upgradability: how a proxy holds storage and delegates execution, and why that separation allows logic swaps. A concrete example will be the deploy-proxy pattern where the proxy address stays constant while implementation addresses change. Third, you will learn to distinguish common proxy patterns — Transparent and UUPS — their upgrade flows, and when each is preferable, including their gas and security trade-offs. Fourth, you will use the OpenZeppelin Upgrades plugin with Hardhat to deploy and manage proxies, observing storage-compatibility safety checks. For each objective we pair a small mnemonic or visual chip to make the idea stick and a verified competency milestone so you know when you've achieved it. As you progress, always ask: who controls the upgrade authority, and will users accept that trust model?

screens.title: Why Upgradability is Needed Despite Immutability
screens.subtitle: The practical problem: bugs, features, and preserving on-chain state

narration.text: Blockchain immutability means that once a contract's bytecode is deployed, it cannot be changed. That property is central to trustless execution, but it creates a maintenance challenge: if a bug is found after deployment or a feature must be added, redeploying a new contract breaks continuity because on-chain state — balances, ownership mappings, and historical references — live at the old address. Users and integrations would need manual migration, which is error-prone. Upgradability solves this by separating the persistent storage from the mutable logic. Practically, you deploy a proxy contract at a stable address to hold state, and you deploy implementation contracts containing logic that the proxy delegates to. When a fix or feature is ready, you deploy a new implementation and update the proxy to point to it. The key constraint is that the proxy's storage layout must remain compatible across implementations, so you can add new variables by appending them but not reorder or change existing state types. For example, if a token contract stores a uint256 at slot zero, changing that slot's type in a later implementation corrupts data. A common misconception is that upgradability removes immutability; it does not. The deployed proxy and the historical implementations remain immutable. Upgradability merely creates an indirection that lets you change which immutable logic contract is used. Consider whether your project's governance and trust model accepts the upgrade authority needed for this pattern.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Upgradability preserves state at one address while allowing the logic to be swapped by pointing the proxy to new implementation contracts.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why Upgradability is Needed
Problem: Immutability vs Maintenance

Immutability protects users but prevents fixing bugs or adding features without migrating state. Migration leads to lost trust and high coordination costs.

Concrete example:
If a deployed contract holds user balances and you discover a bug, redeploying to a new address forces every holder to move funds. An upgrade keeps the same address and preserves balances.
Misconception Check
  • Upgrades do not change past transactions: old implementation bytecode remains immutable.
  • You cannot arbitrarily change storage layout; compatibility rules must be followed.
  • Upgrade authority introduces trust assumptions that must be communicated to users.
Pattern: Proxy + Implementation
Proxy (fixed address)
Holds state variables and a pointer to the current implementation address. Users always interact with this address.
Implementation (swapable)
Contains business logic. Deploy new implementations to add features or fix bugs. The proxy delegates calls using delegatecall, executing implementation code in the proxy context so storage is preserved.
Why it matters

This separation lets teams iterate and fix code while keeping user data intact at the same address, reducing migration friction.

screens.title: How delegatecall Lets Logic Run on Proxy Storage
screens.subtitle: Mechanics of execution and why storage lives in the proxy

narration.text: Delegatecall is the low-level operation that makes upgradable proxies work. When the proxy receives a transaction that it should forward, it reads the current implementation address and performs a delegatecall into that implementation. Delegatecall executes the implementation's code but in the calling contract's context, so storage reads and writes use the proxy's storage slots and the original msg. sender and msg. value are preserved. This is why implementations must not declare constructors that set proxy state; initialization functions are used instead. A concrete example: an implementation function that sets slot zero to a value will write into the proxy's slot zero when invoked via delegatecall. A common pitfall is forgetting to use initialization guards: implementation contracts should disable direct initializers to prevent someone from initializing the implementation itself and hijacking ownership. Another misconception is treating delegatecall as a copy: delegatecall does not copy storage or code; it simply uses the implementation code with the proxy's storage. Why this matters: storage layout between versions must align exactly, otherwise the proxy will read and write incorrect slots and corrupt state. As you design upgradable contracts, write tests that call functions through the proxy and validate that state persists and behaves as expected through an upgrade.

keyIdea.title: Execution detail
keyIdea.text: Delegatecall runs implementation code in the proxy's storage context, preserving msg.sender and storage slots in the proxy.

content.html:
Process Flow › delegatecall Mechanics
Delegatecall flow
  1. Proxy receives transaction and looks up implementation address.
  2. Proxy performs delegatecall to the implementation address with the original calldata.
  3. Implementation code executes but reads/writes storage in the proxy's slots.
  4. Return values go back through the proxy to the caller, preserving msg.sender.
Concrete example
If a retrieve function reads slot zero, and store writes slot zero in the implementation, those operations affect the proxy's storage when invoked through delegatecall.
Misconception

Delegatecall copies nothing; it reuses code on the implementation but applies it to the proxy's storage.

Design implication

Because the implementation works on proxy storage, you must design storage layout carefully and use initializer functions instead of constructors. Also, ensure the implementation disables direct initialization so it cannot be hijacked.

Initialization
Use initializer patterns and call initialize through the proxy.
Disable implementation init
Call disableInitializers in implementation constructor to prevent direct initialization.
Key Takeaway

Treat delegatecall as execution-in-proxy: code runs in the implementation but state changes live in the proxy.

screens.title: Transparent Proxy Pattern
screens.subtitle: Owner vs user call handling and gas considerations

narration.text: The Transparent Proxy pattern solves a key conflict: the proxy itself may expose administrative functions while the implementation exposes user functions that might share names. To avoid name clashes, the transparent proxy checks whether the caller is the owner. If the caller is the owner, the proxy routes calls to proxy-admin functions such as upgrades. If the caller is a non-owner, the proxy unconditionally delegates the call to the implementation. This separation prevents an implementation function from inadvertently shadowing an admin function. The trade-off is that every call must check msg. sender, adding a slight gas overhead to the proxy's fallback path. A concrete example: the proxy may have an upgrade function accessible to the owner. If the implementation also defined a function with the same signature, a regular user might accidentally call it; the transparent proxy prevents that by only delegating non-owner calls. A common misconception is that transparent proxies are always simpler; in fact they add an owner-path inside the proxy, which changes where authorization logic lives. Transparent proxies keep upgrade logic in the proxy rather than the implementation, which can be conceptually clearer but slightly costlier on gas for each user call.

keyIdea.title: Transparent proxy
keyIdea.text: Proxy inspects caller identity: owner calls manage proxy, others are delegated to implementation to avoid function clashes.

content.html:
Comparison › Transparent Proxy
How it works

Proxy checks msg.sender: if owner, handle admin actions on the proxy; otherwise delegate to implementation.

Benefits
  • Prevents implementation-admin function clashes.
  • Clear separation of upgrade control inside proxy.
Drawbacks
  • Extra msg.sender checks on every call add small gas overhead.
  • Upgrade logic centralized in proxy; proxy code must be trusted.
Concrete scenario
Imagine a token implementation that also exposes an admin-only mint function. Using a transparent proxy ensures a non-owner calling 'mint' hits the implementation, while the proxy owner uses admin controls on the proxy to change the implementation pointer instead of running implementation-admin functions directly through the proxy path.
Misconception

The transparent proxy does not make upgrades automatic or safe by itself — it only organizes where upgrade logic runs and avoids name collisions.

screens.title: UUPS Pattern (Universal Upgradeable Proxy Standard)
screens.subtitle: Implementation-led upgrades and improved gas efficiency

narration.text: UUPS flips the responsibility for upgrades: instead of the proxy owning upgrade logic, the implementation contract exposes an upgrade function. The proxy simply delegates all calls, including upgrade calls, to the implementation, and the implementation checks authorization in a function like _authorizeUpgrade. This reduces the proxy's fallback complexity and removes the per-call owner check, making regular user calls slightly more gas efficient. However, this design means that upgrade authorization lives in the implementation; a bug in that authorization or in the implementation itself can make the upgrade path dangerous. For example, if _authorizeUpgrade is implemented incorrectly, an attacker might gain the ability to point the proxy to a malicious implementation. OpenZeppelin's UUPS helpers are tested widely to mitigate this risk, but the conceptual change remains: upgrades are implemented by the logic contract. A common misconception is that UUPS is always superior; in practice you choose based on your team's preference for where upgrade code should live and how you manage audit coverage. If you prefer a thinner proxy and are disciplined with implementation authorization, UUPS offers measurable gas savings for regular calls.

keyIdea.title: UUPS in brief
keyIdea.text: Upgrade function lives in the implementation. Proxy delegates everything, improving gas for normal calls but moving upgrade authorization to the implementation.

content.html:
Comparison › UUPS Pattern
How it works

Implementation exposes an upgrade function; the proxy delegates all calls. Implementation enforces authorization for upgrades.

Benefits
  • Lower gas for user calls due to thinner proxy fallback.
  • Simpler proxy reduces on-chain complexity.
Risks and considerations
  • Upgrade authorization lives in implementation; bugs can brick upgrade path or enable unauthorized upgrades.
  • Audit focus shifts to _authorizeUpgrade and related hooks.
Concrete practice
Implement _authorizeUpgrade with strong access control, often using Ownable or a multisig guard, and include tests that try unauthorized upgrades.

screens.title: OpenZeppelin Upgrades Plugin for Hardhat
screens.subtitle: How to add and configure the plugin in your project

narration.text: OpenZeppelin's Upgrades plugin for Hardhat automates deploying proxies, linking implementations, and performing upgrades while running storage-compatibility checks. To use it you add the plugin to your Hardhat config and to your project dependencies. The plugin exposes a high-level upgrades A P I with functions like deployProxy and upgradeProxy. These functions handle ERC1967 storage slot conventions, emit helpful logs, and integrate checks that throw on incompatible storage changes. A practical example is updating hardhat. config. js to require the plugin, then calling upgrades. deployProxy with the contract factory and constructor-like initializer arguments. Another important step is installing the upgradeable contracts package when using OpenZeppelin's upgradeable base contracts. A common mistake is forgetting to call disableInitializers in the implementation constructor or calling initialize on the implementation directly — both can leave the implementation in an initialized state, which is undesirable. In practice, follow the plugin's guidance, run its tests locally, and check the printed implementation address with upgrades. erc1967. getImplementationAddress to confirm where logic lives. This tooling reduces manual pitfalls but does not replace thoughtful storage design and thorough auditing. OpenZeppelin Upgrades Plugin for Hardhat means the plugin automates proxy lifecycle tasks and enforces storage safety checks, but correct initialization and audit discipline remain essential.. In practical terms, how to add and configure the plugin in your project. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: The plugin automates proxy lifecycle tasks and enforces storage safety checks, but correct initialization and audit discipline remain essential.

Tooling › OpenZeppelin Upgrades for Hardhat
Install and require
npm install @openzeppelin/hardhat-upgrades @openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable
      
// hardhat.config.js
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");
require("@openzeppelin/hardhat-upgrades");
These steps wire the plugin into Hardhat so its high-level API is available in scripts and tasks.
Important practices
  • Use deployProxy and upgradeProxy from the upgrades object.
  • Verify implementation addresses with upgrades.erc1967.getImplementationAddress.
  • Disable initializers in implementation constructors to avoid direct initialization.
Tip

Run the plugin's storage-layout checks as part of CI to detect incompatible changes early.

screens.title: Deploying an Upgradable Proxy with Hardhat
screens.subtitle: deployProxy usage and verifying implementation address

narration.text: Deploying an upgradable contract using the OpenZeppelin Upgrades plugin is straightforward. You create a contract factory with ethers, then call upgrades. deployProxy with initializer arguments and a kind option of 'uups' or 'transparent'. The plugin deploys both the implementation and the proxy, wires them together, and returns a proxy instance you can interact with. A practical example is a Box contract initialized with a value. After deployProxy resolves, you should call upgrades. erc1967. getImplementationAddress with the proxy address to log the implementation address and confirm the deployed target. Remember to call initialize via the proxy to set owner and initial state; do not call initialize on the implementation. A common stumbling block is forgetting to pass the appropriate kind option; the default may not match your intended pattern. Also ensure the implementation uses Initializable and disables constructors using disableInitializers. After deployment, test the proxy's functions to confirm state is stored and behaves as expected. The plugin's logs and the implementation address check are your immediate verification steps after a deploy. Deploying an Upgradable Proxy with Hardhat means use upgrades.deployproxy to deploy proxy and implementation together, then verify the implementation address via upgrades.erc1967.getimplementationaddress.. In practical terms, deployproxy usage and verifying implementation address. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deploy flow
keyIdea.text: Use upgrades.deployProxy to deploy proxy and implementation together, then verify the implementation address via upgrades.erc1967.getImplementationAddress.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Deploying Proxy 
// scripts/deploy-upgradable.js
const { upgrades } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const MyContract = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyContract");
  const myContract = await upgrades.deployProxy(MyContract, [initialArg], { kind: "uups" });
  await myContract.deployed();
  console.log("MyContract deployed to:", myContract.address);
  console.log("Implementation address:", await upgrades.erc1967.getImplementationAddress(myContract.address));
}

main();
Checklist after deploy
  • Confirm proxy address returned by deployProxy.
  • Log and verify the implementation address with erc1967 helper.
  • Interact with retrieve/store functions and verify state is persisted.
Common mistake

Do not call initialize directly on the implementation contract; always initialize through the proxy.

screens.title: Upgrading a Proxy to a New Implementation
screens.subtitle: upgradeProxy example and verifying state preservation

narration.text: Upgrading a proxy uses upgrades. upgradeProxy, which deploys a new implementation and points the proxy to it. You pass the existing proxy address and the new contract factory. After the upgrade completes, the returned object is a wrapper linked to the proxy address but executing new logic. Verify that storage is preserved by calling retrieval methods before and after the upgrade — values that existed under V1 should remain available under V2, provided storage layout rules were respected. It's useful to log the new implementation address with upgrades. erc1967. getImplementationAddress to confirm the change. A concrete script demonstrates this pattern: get the BoxV2 factory, call upgrades. upgradeProxy with the proxy address, and then call retrieve and new V2 functions, like increment, to confirm new behavior. Remember that upgradeProxy verifies storage layout compatibility; if you change existing state variable types or reorder slots, the plugin will throw errors. If that happens, revise your storage changes by appending new variables or migrating state carefully with a custom upgrade routine. Always run automated tests that simulate upgrade paths so you catch incompatibilities locally before pushing to a live network.

keyIdea.title: Upgrade flow
keyIdea.text: Use upgrades.upgradeProxy to point the proxy at a new implementation and verify state persists and new methods are accessible.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Upgrading Proxy 
// scripts/upgrade.js
const { upgrades } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const MyContractV2 = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyContractV2");
  const existingProxyAddress = "0x...";
  const myContractV2 = await upgrades.upgradeProxy(existingProxyAddress, MyContractV2);
  console.log("New implementation:", await upgrades.erc1967.getImplementationAddress(myContractV2.address));
}

main();
Post-upgrade checks
  • Call retrieve() to confirm prior state persists.
  • Call new V2 functions (e.g., increment) to confirm new logic works.
  • Log the implementation address to ensure it changed.
If upgrade fails

An incompatibility error likely means storage layout changed in an unsafe way. Revisit layout changes and use migrations that append variables only.

screens.title: Storage Compatibility Rules
screens.subtitle: Why changing types or order corrupts proxy storage

narration.text: Storage compatibility is the rule set that prevents data corruption when swapping implementations. The proxy holds storage slots in a fixed layout, and implementations operate on those slots via delegatecall. If you change the type of an existing variable, or reorder state variables, their storage slots no longer match previous expectations. That mismatch leads to corrupted values and unpredictable behavior. The safe rules are simple: never remove or reorder existing state variables; do not change a variable's type; append new variables at the end of the existing layout. OpenZeppelin's Upgrades plugin enforces these checks automatically and will reject upgrades that violate layout compatibility. A concrete error case is changing a uint256 to a string—this will typically trigger a storage layout compatibility error because the underlying slot usage differs. For controlled changes, you can introduce a migration function in a new implementation that reads existing slots and writes to new slots in a safe, tested way. A misconception to avoid is thinking the plugin obviates design discipline: it helps, but you still must plan your contract's storage across future versions and document the layout for audits.

keyIdea.title: Storage rule
keyIdea.text: Preserve existing state layout: append new variables but do not reorder or change existing types to maintain compatibility.

content.html:
Definition › Storage Compatibility
Rules you must follow
  • Do not reorder existing state variables.
  • Do not change the type of existing variables.
  • Append new variables at the end of the storage layout.
Example of a breaking change
Changing uint256 value to string value in a new version will likely break storage interpretation and is rejected by the plugin.
Safe migration pattern
If you must alter representation, add new slots and write migration code in a controlled upgrade that copies old values to the new layout, and include tests to verify correctness.
Key Takeaway

Plan storage early and append fields only. Use plugin checks and tests to catch layout problems before upgrading live contracts.

screens.title: Security Considerations and Trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Centralization, trust, attack surface, and complexity

narration.text: Upgradable contracts introduce operational flexibility but also new security and governance challenges. The most visible risk is centralization: the upgrade authority often rests with a single owner or a small multisig. If that key is compromised, an attacker can push a malicious implementation. Consequently, define an upgrade authority model that aligns with your project's trust assumptions — a multisig or on-chain governance can reduce single-key risk. Another attack avenue is buggy upgrade logic inside the implementation, especially in UUPS where _authorizeUpgrade must be robust. An incorrect authorization check can allow unauthorized upgrades or render future upgrades impossible. Storage collisions and layout errors are another source of vulnerabilities that can corrupt balances or permissions across upgrades. Finally, added complexity increases audit surface: upgradable systems require tests for deployment, initialization, and upgrade paths in addition to standard unit tests. Practical defenses include using battle-tested libraries like OpenZeppelin Upgrades, documenting the upgrade process, running automated compatibility checks in CI, and limiting and rotating upgrade authority keys. Always keep a recovery plan and clear disclosure to users about what upgrade authority means for funds they trust to the contract.

keyIdea.title: Security balance
keyIdea.text: Upgradability buys flexibility at the cost of extra attack surface and trust assumptions; mitigate with multisigs, audits, and strict upgrade policies.

content.html:
Security › Trade-offs and Mitigations
Main risks
  • Centralization: compromised upgrade key can deploy malicious implementations.
  • Implementation bugs in upgrade logic, especially for UUPS.
  • Storage layout errors leading to corruption.
Mitigations
  • Use multisig or governance for upgrades.
  • Audit _authorizeUpgrade and initializer handling.
  • Run storage compatibility checks and upgrade tests in CI.
Operational practices
Document upgrade authority, keep keys offline when possible, rotate multisig membership, and publish upgrade plans to allow users to prepare for changes.
Key Takeaway

Adopt defensive governance and tooling to reduce centralized-risk and audit the upgrade path thoroughly before enabling upgrades on mainnet.

screens.title: BoxV1 → BoxV2: Full Deploy and Upgrade Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Example contract, deploy script, and upgrade script explained

narration.text: This walkthrough ties together our examples: BoxV1 is a minimal upgradable contract with an initializer, store and retrieve functions, and UUPS authorization. BoxV2 adds a new state variable and functions while preserving the V1 storage layout by appending the new variable. The deploy script creates the proxy with kind 'uups' and logs the proxy and implementation addresses. The upgrade script deploys BoxV2 and calls upgrades. upgradeProxy to point the proxy at the new implementation. To validate, interact with retrieve before and after the upgrade and call new V2 methods like increment and getNewValue to confirm they function and that previous state persists. Important safety steps include calling _disableInitializers in the implementation constructors to prevent direct initialization, using Initializable and OwnableUpgradeable, and ensuring _authorizeUpgrade uses onlyOwner. Also test that new variables initialize safely, and that upgrading on a testnet preserves the retrieve value. A common misconception is thinking adding any variable is safe; you must append them. In the lab, we practice these steps and verify outputs in the terminal to build confidence that the upgrade process preserves state and exposes new behavior at the same proxy address.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Deploy BoxV1 via deployProxy, upgrade to BoxV2 with upgradeProxy, and confirm state and new behavior persist at the same proxy address.

content.html:
Hands-on Lab › Box V1 to V2
BoxV1 (key parts)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/proxy/utils/Initializable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/access/OwnableUpgradeable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/proxy/utils/UUPSUpgradeable.sol";

contract BoxV1 is Initializable, OwnableUpgradeable, UUPSUpgradeable {
    uint256 private _value;

    constructor() { _disableInitializers(); }

    function initialize(uint256 value) initializer public {
        __Ownable_init();
        __UUPSUpgradeable_init();
        _value = value;
    }

    function store(uint256 value) public onlyOwner { _value = value; }
    function retrieve() public view returns (uint256) { return _value; }
    function _authorizeUpgrade(address newImplementation) internal override onlyOwner {}
}
BoxV2 additions
// BoxV2 appends state and adds functions
contract BoxV2 is Initializable, OwnableUpgradeable, UUPSUpgradeable {
    uint256 private _value;
    uint256 private _newValue; // appended safely

    constructor() { _disableInitializers(); }

    function initialize(uint256 value) initializer public {
        __Ownable_init();
        __UUPSUpgradeable_init();
        _value = value;
        _newValue = 0;
    }

    function increment() public onlyOwner { _value++; }
    function getNewValue() public view returns (uint256) { return _newValue; }
    function setNewValue(uint256 val) public onlyOwner { _newValue = val; }
    function _authorizeUpgrade(address newImplementation) internal override onlyOwner {}
}
Check

Run deploy script, note proxy address, call retrieve, upgrade to V2, then call retrieve and new functions to confirm persistence and added behavior.

screens.title: Recommended Upgrade Workflow and Tests
screens.subtitle: A checklist for deploying, testing, and releasing upgrades

narration.text: A disciplined workflow reduces risk when performing upgrades. Start in a feature branch and write both unit tests and upgrade-path tests that simulate state before and after an upgrade. Locally deploy the proxy and implementation to a local or testnet instance, initialize through the proxy, and run the tests that exercise both old and new functions. Use the OpenZeppelin plugin's storage-layout checks as part of CI so incompatible changes fail early. Before production, prepare a deployment plan that includes multisig approvals or governance proposals, a changelog describing behavior changes, and rollback steps in case of regressions. On deploy day, deploy implementation and upgrade in a controlled window, then run integration smoke tests and verify balances, permissions, and key invariants. After upgrade, monitor for unexpected events and be ready to pause or revert if a serious problem appears. A common oversight is skipping upgrade-path tests; these are essential because they catch subtle storage or access-control issues that unit tests alone might miss. Treat the upgrade like a release: rehearsed, tested, and observable. Recommended Upgrade Workflow and Tests means treat upgrades as production releases: test upgrade paths, use ci checks, define governance approvals, and monitor after deployment.. In practical terms, a checklist for deploying, testing, and releasing upgrades. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Treat upgrades as production releases: test upgrade paths, use CI checks, define governance approvals, and monitor after deployment.

content.html:
Process Flow › Upgrade Workflow
Checklist
  1. Write unit tests and upgrade-path tests that deploy V1, initialize via proxy, then upgrade to V2 and verify state and new APIs.
  2. Run OpenZeppelin storage-layout checks in CI to detect incompatible changes.
  3. Use multisig or governance for upgrade approvals; prepare a deploy plan and changelog.
  4. Deploy implementation, run upgrade in a controlled window, then execute smoke tests and monitoring scripts.
  5. Have rollback or mitigation steps documented before any mainnet upgrade.

screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from the chapter

narration.text: Keep three core ideas in mind as you apply upgradability. First, immutability remains true: deployed bytecode is immutable. Upgradability is an indirection pattern that preserves state at a fixed proxy address while swapping logic contracts. Second, storage compatibility is critical: do not reorder or change types of existing state variables; append new ones. OpenZeppelin's tooling checks help, but you must design layout up front. Third, upgrade governance defines trust: decide who can upgrade and enforce it with multisig, governance, or strict authorization hooks. Each of these choices has operational and security consequences that you must document and test. These three principles — preserving state, keeping storage compatible, and defining secure upgrade authority — will guide safe use of proxy patterns in real projects. narration.text: Use this quick reference while developing and auditing upgrades.
